name: Zinc for body odor

lead: Zinc is an essential mineral sold as an over-the-counter supplement, and some online discussion links it to reduced body odour. The hoped-for payoff is a less noticeable natural smell.

Body odour is generally attributed to bacteria acting on sweat. The reference pages consulted do not mention zinc in connection with body odour, and the mechanism proponents suggest is not documented there. Oral zinc is studied and used for deficiency.

paras: People take zinc as a daily supplement, often in forms such as gluconate or acetate, alongside other grooming habits. Users who try it for odour typically judge the result over a few weeks.

The sources consulted do not assess risks for this use. Oral zinc is used for deficiency repletion, and people with medical conditions or on other medications may want to check with a clinician first.

chain: Claimed change in sweat or bacteria
angle.text: Supplement and appearance communities circulate the idea that taking zinc orally changes sweat or skin bacteria and so reduces body odour. Zinc is studied for deficiency, and the sources consulted do not cover an odour effect.

lead: Zinc for body odor refers to the idea, circulated in supplement and appearance communities, that zinc can reduce underarm and body odor and so help people smell cleaner. Zinc is an essential trace mineral; oral forms such as zinc gluconate and zinc acetate are used to treat or prevent zinc deficiency, and zinc compounds also appear in topical products. [1][2]

Body odor is attributed mainly to skin bacteria acting on apocrine sweat: Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus species convert sweat compounds into smelly molecules such as butyric acid, isovaleric acid and thioalcohols. [3] Topical zinc has been studied in this setting. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in Acta Dermato-Venereologica in 2020, 30 healthy volunteers had one armpit treated with zinc oxide and the other with placebo for 13 days. Zinc oxide reduced total bacterial growth and counts of Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus hominis, and participants reported less self-perceived malodour with it than with placebo (p = 0.005). [4]
A 1977 letter in Archives of Dermatology addressed zinc sulfate and axillary perspiration odor. [5] No trial of oral zinc supplements for body odor was found.

paras: Apocrine glands, which become active at puberty and are concentrated in the armpits, are the main contributor to body odor, and skin bacteria metabolize their secretions into odorants. Genetics, diet, health and medication also contribute. [3] Standard treatments listed include antiperspirants with aluminum chloride, deodorants, bathing and, for severe cases, surgery. [3]

Wikipedia's zinc deficiency article lists acne, eczema, dry skin and hair thinning among signs of deficiency, and says severe deficiency can dull taste and smell. [1] It does not link zinc to body odor.

The 2020 trial found that zinc oxide lowered axillary bacterial counts and that volunteers rated their own malodour lower, although skin-surface pH rose. In laboratory tests, 19 Corynebacterium strains were inhibited at 400 mg/l or less. [4] A 1983 deodorant-evaluation paper in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science mentions zinc ricinoleate as an odor absorber. [6]
The topical zinc oxide trial described above is the main human study found. [4] No studies found of oral zinc supplements for body odor.
